passage: I'm Joseph, and I was at my cousin's wedding when I noticed Manjula standing by a pillar with a glass of water. Her grandmother had died a month before. The floor was crowded with dancing relatives, and the drums were loud. Two cousins pulled at Manjula's hands. “Come on, Manju!” An aunt called, “Enough sadness now, it's a wedding!” Manjula smiled with her mouth only and stepped back. Her mother, across the hall, looked at her and said nothing. I can't say for certain what Manjula felt. But she stayed by that pillar for a long time, and when the song changed, she slipped outside alone.

qa.q: What was Manjula holding while she stood by the pillar?
qa.a: Manjula was holding a glass of water.

qa.q: What might Manjula be feeling as she smiles with her mouth only and steps back?
qa.a: Manjula may be feeling doubly alone, with grief made sharper by everyone else's joy, though Joseph says the inner feeling can't be known for sure.

qa.q: What could a relative do at the wedding to help Manjula without pushing her?
qa.a: A relative could sit near her, ask softly if she wants company or fresh air, and not urge her to dance.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Manjula's mother to look across the hall and say nothing?
qa.a: Manjula's mother may have been grieving too and unsure how to help, or careful not to make a scene, though the passage does not say.

grounding: A teenager who is grieving watches others celebrate at a wedding and feels alone, seen by an observer.

passage:
Saturday. Nikita's class won the inter-school quiz, and the team went for pizza afterwards. Nikita had missed the practice sessions, so nobody had told her. She saw the photos that night on her phone: everyone laughing, one empty seat at the end.
Monday. In the corridor, groups were replaying the day. “You should've seen Kabir's face!” Nikita walked past with her bag held close. Vinita glanced at her but got pulled into the laughter.
Thursday. Vinita found Nikita at the library window. “I saw the photos,” she said. “I should have called. Want to come for tea after school? Just us.” Nikita nodded, not quite smiling.

qa.q: What did Nikita see on her phone on Saturday night?
qa.a: Nikita saw photos of everyone laughing, with one empty seat at the end.

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling as she walked past the groups in the corridor on Monday?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt left out and alone, since everyone else was celebrating and the bag held close suggests she was guarding herself.

qa.q: What did Vinita do on Thursday that helped?
qa.a: Vinita named it, said she should have called and offered tea, just the two of them, which left Nikita room to say yes at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Vinita have been feeling on Monday when Vinita glanced at Nikita but got pulled into the laughter?
qa.a: Vinita may have felt torn and a little guilty, noticing Nikita but carried along by the group's joy.

grounding: A teenager who is excluded watches others celebrate and feels doubly alone, across a few days.

passage: Binita, you asked why I skipped the Eid party at your place. I'm sorry. This is Parveen being honest. It was our first Eid since Abbu died in March. The whole lane was lit up, kids running around in new clothes, everyone's phones buzzing with 'Eid Mubarak'. My cousins were laughing in the courtyard, and I wanted to laugh too, but every sweet dish smelled like him. Ammi made sheer khurma anyway, and we both stood in the kitchen not eating it. When your message came saying 'come, everyone's here!', I felt more alone than ever. Not because of you. Just because everyone was so happy, and I couldn't find the door into it. Can we meet next week, just the two of us?

qa.q: When did Abbu die?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: Why did Binita's message make Parveen feel more alone?
qa.a: Seeing everyone so happy made Parveen's grief sharper, and Parveen felt shut outside the joy, unable to 'find the door into it'.

qa.q: What could Binita do next time?
qa.a: Meet Parveen quietly, just the two of them as Parveen asks, and let Parveen rejoin celebrations at Parveen's own pace.

qa.q: How might Ammi experience that first Eid?
qa.a: She made sheer khurma anyway, perhaps to keep the tradition, but stood in the kitchen not eating it, likely sharing Parveen's grief.

grounding: A grieving teenager watches a whole community celebrate and feels doubly alone.

passage: Monday: the class group chat buzzed with plans for Hafsa's birthday at the bowling alley. Deepika, new since January, scrolled up and down. Her name wasn't on the list. She told herself it was a mistake. Saturday: photos started appearing. Twelve classmates in matching caps, laughing at the lanes. Downstairs, Deepika's mother was cooking biryani for a cousin's engagement, the house full of happy noise, and Deepika sat on her bed, feeling like the only quiet thing in two celebrations. Tuesday: Hafsa stopped her after class. 'I'm really sorry. My mother made the list from last year's class. I only noticed on Saturday.' Deepika shrugged, but her shoulders loosened a little. 'Next time,' Hafsa said, 'you're on it first.'

qa.q: Where was Hafsa's birthday?
qa.a: At the bowling alley.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel on Saturday, sitting on her bed?
qa.a: She felt hurt and doubly alone, left out of the party photos and unable to join the happy noise of her own house.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that helped, and what could she do next?
qa.a: She apologised honestly and explained the mistake; next she could invite Deepika to something soon, not only 'next time'.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel after noticing on Saturday?
qa.a: Likely guilty and embarrassed that a new classmate had been left out of her celebration.

grounding: Over a week a newly arrived teenager, left out of a celebration, feels doubly alone amid others' joy.

passage: Disha, you're sad your friends are all at the New Year party while you're stuck here with your cast? Let your Grandpa Francis tell you something. When I was fifteen, my mother died in November. That Christmas, our whole street in Goa was lit with stars and paper lanterns. The carol singers came to every house, and the neighbours danced all night. I sat on the balcao, the front porch, and watched. Every carol felt like a stone in my chest. My father was inside with my aunts. Then old Mr Rodrigues from two houses down came and sat next to me with two plates of cake. He didn't ask me to sing. He just said, 'Your mother loved this song.' I cried, and he let me. That was the first time the lights didn't feel cruel.

qa.q: When did young Francis's mother die?
qa.a: In November.

qa.q: What did the carols feel like to young Francis?
qa.a: Each carol felt like a stone in his chest; he was grieving and felt shut out of the street's joy.

qa.q: What did Mr Rodrigues do that made a difference in the story?
qa.a: He sat beside young Francis with cake, didn't push him to join in, and gently mentioned his mother, which let him cry.

qa.q: What might Mr Rodrigues have noticed that others missed?
qa.a: That a grieving boy was alone on the balcao while the whole street celebrated, and needed company, not cheering up.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how a street's celebration sharpened his grief as a teenager, until a neighbour sat with him.

passage: Rain drove the school's annual day into the cramped assembly hall, and the noise doubled: drums, whistles, the Class 11 dance crew shrieking about costumes. Tenzin stood by the back wall holding the sound cables he had promised to manage. Three weeks ago his Momo-la had died, and he had come back to school early because staying home was worse. Now everyone was so happy it felt like a wall he couldn't climb. When the whole hall sang for the principal's birthday, he mouthed the words and felt lonelier than he had at the cremation. Avni, from the dance crew, came over with a paper plate of jalebis. She didn't say "cheer up". She just stood beside him, held the other end of the cable, and stayed until the lights went off.

qa.q: Why was the annual day held in the assembly hall?
qa.a: Rain drove it into the cramped assembly hall.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel while the hall sang for the principal?
qa.a: He felt lonelier than at the cremation; everyone's happiness felt like a wall between him and them.

qa.q: Why did Avni's approach help more than telling Tenzin to cheer up?
qa.a: She stayed beside him and shared his task without asking him to feel happy, so he had company in his sadness.

qa.q: How might the celebration look to the dance crew?
qa.a: To them it is a noisy, exciting day, and most probably don't notice that the same noise is painful for someone grieving.

grounding: Shows a grieving teenager watching a school celebration and feeling doubly alone, as shared joy sharpens his sorrow.
